We first validate the effectiveness of our proposed models on the MNIST simulated data. We then apply these models to the TCCA breast cancer multi-omics data for overall survival prediction. RESULTS: For breast cancer overall survival prediction, the integration of DNA methylation and miRNA expression achieves the best overall performance of 0.641 ± 0.031 with ConcatAE, and 0.63 ± 0.081 with CrossAE. Both strategies outperform baseline single-modality models using only DNA methylation (0.583 ± 0.058) or miRNA expression (0.616 ± 0.057). CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, we achieve improved overall survival prediction performance by utilizing either the complementary or consensus information among multi-omics data. The proposed ConcatAE and CrossAE models can inspire future deep representation-based multi-omics integration techniques. We believe these novel multi-omics integration models can benefit the personalized diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer patients.
papers.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making

papers.title: The Reasoning Paradox in Scientific Sandboxes: Why Extended Reasoning Fails in Autonomous Bioinformatics and How to Fix It.
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) trained with extended reasoning, such as DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, have established state-of-the-art benchmarks in formal logic, competitive programming, and mathematics. In interactive, empirical scientific sandboxes, however, their efficacy remains counter-intuitive. In the Bioinformatics Benchmark (BixBench), extended reasoning models paradoxically degraded in multi-turn environments, leading benchmark authors to exclude them from primary agentic evaluations. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic forensic audit of the internal cognitive monologue ( ... ) of open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) and matched instruction-tuned controls (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) deployed inside containerized computational biology sandboxes on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Our forensic analysis uncovers two distinct systemic failure modes: (1) The PubMed Prior Trap, in which reasoning models engage in epistemic rationalization within their cognitive stream, falsely convincing themselves that empirical datasets are missing and substituting empirical computation with speculative literature recall (e.g., estimating adjusted p-values based on "typical experimental outcomes"); and (2) Tag Language Nesting Collisions, in which models conflate agent-level XML action tags with Python syntax, producing terminal interpreter syntax errors. To resolve this paradox, we introduce Dual Track Decoupled Reasoning (DTDR), an agent scaffolding architecture that evicts internal cognitive monologues from multi-turn history, injects strict empirical grounding guardrails, and dynamically intercepts runtime tool invocations. On a stratified diagnostic benchmark spanning single-cell RNA-seq, bulk differential expression (DESeq2), and genomic variant prioritization (n=22 per arm), DTDR rescues the 14B reasoning model from 0.0% to 9.09% accuracy (2/22), doubling the performance of the matched non-reasoning coder control (4.55%, 1/22) while slashing code execution errors by 81% (13.6% vs. 72.7%) and reducing average steps to solution by 66% (1.77 vs. 5.18 steps). All replication pipelines, prompts, and trajectory manifests are openly released.

papers.title: Massively parallel quantification and prediction of monomeric protein yield in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Obtaining sufficient quantities of purified proteins in their intended molecular states is essential for biological research and protein engineering. Advances in computational protein design have expanded the functional capabilities of de novo proteins and accelerated candidate generation. However, reliable methods for ranking expected monomeric yield of candidate de novo designs, including molecular binders, fluorescent proteins and enzymes, have yet to be established. Standardized measurements of monomeric yield across diverse sequences remain scarce, limiting our understanding of its determinants and the development of accurate predictors for candidate selection. Here we developed a scalable pooled assay combining peptide barcodes, size-exclusion chromatography and mass spectrometry to quantify monomeric yield for over 39,000 natural protein domain variants, de novo proteins and nanobodies under uniform and standardized Escherichia coli production conditions. We used this dataset to (1) quantify the relationship between folding stability and monomeric yield, (2) benchmark inverse-folding methods, (3) evaluate the utility of structure-prediction confidence metrics in selecting high-yield design candidates, and (4) identify sequence and structural patterns in nanobodies associated with monomeric yield and monomer-to-dimer yield ratios. We further developed ESMC-MonoYield, a protein language model fine-tuned to predict monomeric yield from amino acid sequence alone, and prospectively demonstrated enrichment of high-yield candidates among BindCraft-designed binders. Our approach enables standardized, large-scale measurement of monomeric yield across diverse proteins, and establishes monomeric yield as a sequence-encoded property that can be learned, predicted and ultimately designed.

papers.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root.
papers.abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

papers.title: Integrated multi-omics analysis of ovarian cancer using variational autoencoders
papers.abstract: Cancer is a complex disease that deregulates cellular functions at various molecular levels (e.g., DNA, RNA, and proteins). Integrated multi-omics analysis of data from these levels is necessary to understand the aberrant cellular functions accountable for cancer and its development. In recent years, Deep Learning (DL) approaches have become a useful tool in integrated multi-omics analysis of cancer data. However, high dimensional multi-omics data are generally imbalanced with too many molecular features and relatively few patient samples. This imbalance makes a DL based integrated multi-omics analysis difficult. DL-based dimensionality reduction technique, including variational autoencoder (VAE), is a potential solution to balance high dimensional multi-omics data. However, there are few VAE-based integrated multi-omics analyses, and they are limited to pancancer. In this work, we did an integrated multi-omics analysis of ovarian cancer using the compressed features learned through VAE and an improved version of VAE, namely Maximum Mean Discrepancy VAE (MMD-VAE). First, we designed and developed a DL architecture for VAE and MMD-VAE. Then we used the architecture for mono-omics, integrated di-omics and tri-omics data analysis of ovarian cancer through cancer samples identification, molecular subtypes clustering and classification, and survival analysis. The results show that MMD-VAE and VAE-based compressed features can respectively classify the transcriptional subtypes of the TCGA datasets with an accuracy in the range of 93.2-95.5% and 87.1-95.7%. Also, survival analysis results show that VAE and MMD-VAE based compressed representation of omics data can be used in cancer prognosis. Based on the results, we can conclude that (i) VAE and MMD-VAE outperform existing dimensionality reduction techniques, (ii) integrated multi-omics analyses perform better or similar compared to their mono-omics counterparts, and (iii) MMD-VAE performs better than VAE in most omics dataset.

papers.title: Kinetics and Evolution-guided Design of High Fidelity CRISPR-Cas Endonucleases
papers.abstract: Finding high-fidelity CRISPR-Cas variants is critical for both the precision of in vitro DNA detection and the safety of in vivo gene-editing therapeutics. However, the large size of the Cas enzymes and the distinct selection criteria between its natural evolution and clinical practice lead to extensive experimental trials and limited success rate for de novo design, directed evolution and protein language model (PLM)-based filtering. Here, we present a physics-driven, PLM-assisted approach that utilizes atomistic molecular dynamics simulations and automated path searching to efficiently obtain the atom-level kinetic insights, including the transition state structures, for the conformational changes of R-loop formation that dictate the off-target DNA recognition and cleavage by Cas. We show that these kinetic insights can pinpoint the fidelity-diminishing protein residues during the early stage of target recognition. Integrated with PLM-filtering of the mutants on these sites, this approach identified high-fidelity SpyCas9 and FnCas12a variants (4.49-fold and 6.69-fold increase respectively from wild-type), surpassing previously reported counterparts at minimal cost of only a few wet-lab validations (cellular genome-editing and ribonucleoprotein cleavage assays respectively).

papers.title: irAEGIS: Pathway-guided interpretable prediction of immune-related adverse events
papers.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are major complications of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and remain difficult to predict prior to treatment initiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to characterize immune states associated with future irAE development. However, translating single-cell measurements into accurate and biologically interpretable patient-level risk predictions remains challenging. Existing approaches typically aggregate cellular profiles into patient-level summaries, thereby obscuring cell type specific signals, or rely on complex deep-learning architectures that offer limited insight into the biological pathways and mechanisms underlying their predictions. Here, we present irAEGIS, a pathway-guided interpretable model for predicting irAE risk from pre-treatment scRNA-seq data. irAEGIS incorporates prior biological knowledge through gene set constrained representation learning, aggregates pathway activities within individual cell types, and integrates cell type specific risk signals through a hierarchical prediction framework. This design enables predictions to be decomposed into contributions from individual cell types, pathways, and genes, providing interpretable explanations across multiple biological resolutions. Across simulated datasets and independent pre-treatment ICI cohorts, irAEGIS consistently outperformed seven existing methods. Beyond predictive performance, irAEGIS identified biologically coherent immune programs associated with irAE risk. In non-small cell lung cancer, irAEGIS highlighted neutrophil-associated inflammatory pathways linked to future irAE development, whereas in melanoma, it identified apoptotic and immune activation pathways in CD8+ NKT-like cells associated with severe irAEs. These findings were independently supported by pathway enrichment, cell-cell communication, and trajectory analyses. Together, irAEGIS provides a biologically informed and interpretable model for linking single-cell immune states to patient outcomes, enabling both accurate risk prediction and mechanistic insight into immune-related adverse events. More broadly, irAEGIS establishes a general strategy for interpretable phenotype prediction and biological discovery from single-cell transcriptomic data.

papers.title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
papers.abstract: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

papers.title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
papers.abstract: \textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. \textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \\textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at \url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

papers.title: DeepOmix: A scalable and interpretable multi-omics deep learning framework and application in cancer survival analysis
papers.abstract: Integrative analysis of multi-omics data can elucidate valuable insights into complex molecular mechanisms for various diseases. However, due to their different modalities and high dimension, utilizing and integrating different types of omics data suffers from great challenges. There is an urgent need to develop a powerful method to improve survival prediction and detect functional gene modules from multi-omics data. To deal with these problems, we present DeepOmix (a scalable and interpretable multi-Omics Deep learning framework and application in cancer survival analysis), a flexible, scalable, and interpretable method for extracting relationships between the clinical survival time and multi-omics data based on a deep learning framework. DeepOmix enables the non-linear combination of variables from different omics datasets and incorporates prior biological information defined by users (such as signaling pathways and tissue networks). Benchmark experiments demonstrate that DeepOmix outperforms the other five cutting-edge prediction methods. Besides, Lower Grade Glioma (LGG) is taken as the case study to perform the prognosis prediction and illustrate the functional module nodes which are associated with the prognostic result in the prediction model.

papers.title: Identification of gene kinetics patterns improves RNA velocity and cell fate prediction using JuloVelo
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA velocity has transformed our capacity to predict future cell states from sequencing snapshots, but existing methods rely on constant or binary kinetic assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneous splicing dynamics of cellular differentiation. Here we present JuloVelo, a deep learning framework that demonstrates that identifying gene kinetics patterns to initialize neural network training dramatically improves RNA velocity model performance. By pre-determining whether each gene follows a Circle, Complete induction, or Complete repression pattern across cellular differentiation, JuloVelo initializes training with pattern-matched, pre-trained network weights, effectively guiding the cell-specific kinetics optimization away from biologically implausible parameter regimes. Additionally, JuloVelo demonstrates that multiome datasets can also be processed and modeled by utilizing promoter chromatin accessibility to guide kinetics pre-determination, and integrates an in silico perturbation framework to simulate transcription factor modulation on cell fate. Validated across eight datasets spanning erythrogenesis, neurogenesis, and endocrinogenesis, JuloVelo consistently outperformed constant-rate and cell-specific models, resolving the entire five-lineage differentiation program in hippocampal neurogenesis. Multiome processing improved both intrinsic and extrinsic velocity stability, and JuloVelo reduced computational execution time by approximately 70% compared to cellDancer. JuloVelo is available as an open-source package at https://github.com/jhlabtw/JuloVelo.jl.

papers.title: Glycosyltransferases: Mining, engineering and applications in biosynthesis of glycosylated plant natural products
papers.abstract: UDP-Glycosyltransferases (UGTs) catalyze the transfer of nucleotide-activated sugars to specific acceptors, among which the GT1 family enzymes are well-known for their function in biosynthesis of natural product glycosides. Elucidating GT function represents necessary step in metabolic engineering of aglycone glycosylation to produce drug leads, cosmetics, nutrients and sweeteners. In this review, we systematically summarize the phylogenetic distribution and catalytic diversity of plant GTs. We also discuss recent progress in the identification of novel GT candidates for synthesis of plant natural products (PNPs) using multi-omics technology and deep learning predicted models. We also highlight recent advances in rational design and directed evolution engineering strategies for new or improved GT functions. Finally, we cover recent breakthroughs in the application of GTs for microbial biosynthesis of some representative glycosylated PNPs, including flavonoid glycosides (fisetin 3-O-glycosides, astragalin, scutellarein 7-O-glucoside), terpenoid glycosides (rebaudioside A, ginsenosides) and polyketide glycosides (salidroside, polydatin).

papers.title: Evaluation of large language models for discovery of gene set function
papers.abstract: Abstract Gene set analysis is a mainstay of functional genomics, but it relies on manually curated databases of gene functions that are incomplete and unaware of biological context. Here we evaluate the ability of OpenAI’s GPT-4, a Large Language Model (LLM), to develop hypotheses about common gene functions from its embedded biomedical knowledge. We created a GPT-4 pipeline to label gene sets with names that summarize their consensus functions, substantiated by analysis text and citations. Benchmarking against named gene sets in the Gene Ontology, GPT-4 generated very similar names in 50% of cases, while in most remaining cases it recovered the name of a more general concept. In gene sets discovered in ‘omics data, GPT-4 names were more informative than gene set enrichment, with supporting statements and citations that largely verified in human review. The ability to rapidly synthesize common gene functions positions LLMs as valuable functional genomics assistants.

papers.title: Beyond Better Models: Barriers and a Path Forward in Generalisable TCR Antigen Specificity Prediction
papers.abstract: T cells are at the centre of adaptive immunity, protecting the organism against infection and cancer. T cell receptors (TCRs), expressed on the surface of T cells, enable the recognition of target cells through interactions with peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecules. Reliable, large-scale mapping of TCRs to their cognate pMHCs remains a holy grail of modern systems immunology, with far-reaching implications for cancer immunotherapy, vaccine development, and the understanding and treatment of autoimmune diseases. While exhaustive experimental mapping remains intractable due to the enormous combinatorial sequence space of TCRs and pMHCs, computational approaches offer a promising alternative. Consequently, we have witnessed increasingly sophisticated computational models of TCR antigen specificity, from small neural networks to deep generative models and large protein language models. However, several independent benchmarks have shown that these models, despite their size and sophistication, largely fail to generalise to TCRs or pMHCs not present in the data available during model development. Here, we investigate possible reasons for this and suggest a path forward to generalisable TCR:pMHC prediction. First, our analysis of the largest public repositories of TCR:pMHC data reveals significant biases towards a small number of antigens and MHC molecules, sparse sampling of TCR sequence space per pMHC, as well as inconsistencies and inaccuracies in data collation. Second, we show the importance of carefully setting up model evaluation to measure discrimination based on antigen specificity instead of confounding factors present in the evaluation data. Finally, we highlight the need for and propose how best to match the evaluation metric with the specific downstream application of the predictions. Our investigation suggests that we, as a community, need more representative and better curated data, and a robust set of metrics and benchmarks to guide future model development towards generalisable TCR:pMHC specificity prediction.

papers.title: GeneAgent: self-verification language agent for gene-set analysis using domain databases
papers.abstract: Gene set knowledge discovery is essential for advancing human functional genomics. Recent studies have shown promising performance by harnessing the power of Large Language Models (LLMs) on this task. Nonetheless, their results are subject to several limitations common in LLMs such as hallucinations. In response, we present GeneAgent, a first-of-its-kind language agent featuring self-verification capability. It autonomously interacts with various biological databases and leverages relevant domain knowledge to improve accuracy and reduce hallucination occurrences. Benchmarking on 1,106 gene sets from different sources, GeneAgent consistently outperforms standard GPT-4 by a significant margin. Moreover, a detailed manual review confirms the effectiveness of the self-verification module in minimizing hallucinations and generating more reliable analytical narratives. To demonstrate its practical utility, we apply GeneAgent to seven novel gene sets derived from mouse B2905 melanoma cell lines, with expert evaluations showing that GeneAgent offers novel insights into gene functions and subsequently expedites knowledge discovery.

papers.title: Sex-based differences in fibrosis markers in human abdominal aortic aneurysms
papers.abstract: Background: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are a complex degenerative vascular disease. The role of fibrosis in AAA progression is unclear. Our study evaluated the impact of fibroblast activation protein (FAP), collagen, and vimentin on AAA fibrosis and progression. We hypothesized that FAP may influence fibrosis and disease severity in AAA, with potential sex-specific differences. Study Design: Multi-centered transcriptomic analysis of aortic samples from 15 human AAA and 5 non-AAA was performed to evaluate cell-specific fibrosis gene expression profiles. Histopathological and molecular analysis of 26 male and female AAA samples (mAAA and fAAA) and 29 male and female normal abdominal aortas (mNAA and fNAA) was performed to assess whole-tissue fibrosis markers and signaling. Results: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis identified eight major cell clusters with distinct sex-based distributions. Although vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and fibroblast clusters had reduced counts in both male and female AAAs, they more highly expressed FAP and COL1A1 genes, particularly in females. Whole-tissue analysis demonstrated elevated extracellular matrix deposits with markedly increased collagen type 1 in both mAAA and fAAA. Alpha-smooth muscle actin (-SMA)-positive VSMCs were also reduced in mAAA and fAAA, but FAP was notably elevated, and robustly in fAAA. FAP-positive fibroblasts in fAAA exhibited increased expression of fibrosis markers, suggesting a unique pro-fibrotic phenotype. Conclusion: Our study reveals a sex-based difference in AAA tissue, with elevated fibrosis markers and increased FAP levels in females, suggesting its significant role in disease progression. These findings underscore the potential of FAP as a unique tissue biomarker for AAAs and warrants further investigation into novel targeted therapies that aim to stabilize AAAs, particularly in female patients.

papers.title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.

papers.title: DPLM: Dynamics-aware Protein Language Model via contrastive learning between sequence and molecular dynamics simulation trajectory
papers.abstract: Protein dynamics captures the interactions between residues and the conformational changes they undergo. Encoding such information could enhance a deep learning model's ability to predict protein properties. Here we introduce a dynamics-aware protein language model (DPLM) that encodes protein dynamics into a sequence-derived representation. We represent each molecular dynamics (MD) trajectory as a sequence of backbone C contact maps and encode it with a Video Vision Transformer (ViViT). We then align the ViViT-derived dynamics embedding with the ESM2-derived sequence embedding using dual-view contrastive learning. The root-mean-square fluctuation correlation and dynamic cross-correlation matrix reconstruction confirm that contrastive learning incorporates dynamics information into the sequence embedding. We applied DPLM as a protein representation backbone for predicting diverse dynamics-related downstream tasks, including liquid-liquid phase separation, cryptic-site detection, and mutation effect on protein thermal stability. DPLM shows strong performance, especially where the evolutionary or structural signal is weak. These results show that learning the geometry of molecular motion yields transferable dynamic information that complements the evolutionary and structural features of existing PLMs.

papers.title: Using neural networks for reducing the dimensions of single-cell RNA-Seq data
papers.abstract: While only recently developed, the ability to profile expression data in single cells (scRNA-Seq) has already led to several important studies and findings. However, this technology has also raised several new computational challenges. These include questions about the best methods for clustering scRNA-Seq data, how to identify unique group of cells in such experiments, and how to determine the state or function of specific cells based on their expression profile. To address these issues we develop and test a method based on neural networks (NN) for the analysis and retrieval of single cell RNA-Seq data. We tested various NN architectures, some of which incorporate prior biological knowledge, and used these to obtain a reduced dimension representation of the single cell expression data. We show that the NN method improves upon prior methods in both, the ability to correctly group cells in experiments not used in the training and the ability to correctly infer cell type or state by querying a database of tens of thousands of single cell profiles. Such database queries (which can be performed using our web server) will enable researchers to better characterize cells when analyzing heterogeneous scRNA-Seq samples.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
papers.abstract: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Profiling Reveals Neuronal Metabolic Collapse During the Transition to Alzheimer's Disease Dementia
papers.abstract: Current Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathological metrics, including Thal phasing, and Braak staging, often do not accurately predict cognitive status: many cognitively resilient individuals have substantial pathological burdens, whereas some patients with dementia show minimal classical AD pathology. Here, we addressed this discrepancy by investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying AD dementia using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and single-nucleus multiome datasets. To eliminate cross-modality scaling artifacts and compositional biases inherent in neurodegenerative tissues, we normalized the datasets using our novel framework, bypassing scaling issues of conventional methods that may obscure critical biological signals of interest. We identified neuron-specific suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and their upstream mitochondrial biogenesis signaling (MBS) as primary drivers of clinical dementia. By integrating multi-omic quantitative trait loci, genome-wide association studies, and epigenomic profiles, we delineated genetic and epigenetic changes underlying MBS suppression. This study provides a systematic genomic framework for understanding the mechanisms of cognitive resilience.

papers.title: Characterisation of cis-regulatory elements and genome wide enhancer prediction in Heliconiini butterflies
papers.abstract: The large-scale annotation and spatiotemporal characterisation of cis-regulatory promoters and enhancers remain limited in many non-model organisms, largely due to fragmented availability of multiomic datasets across species and developmental conditions. Heliconius butterflies, which have been used to investigate wing development and patterning, have provided key insights into the genetic architecture underlying morphological diversification and adaptive pigmentation. Despite this, we are limited in what we understand of how cis-regulatory dynamics drive phenotypic wing patterning variation. Here, by re-analysing and re-evaluating available data, we present a comprehensive new description of a cis-regulatory atlas for Heliconius wing development by integrating chromatin accessibility dynamics (ATAC-seq) with histone modification profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me3). High-confidence peak sets enabled robust annotation of promoters and enhancers, revealing regulatory distributions consistent with canonical regulatory organisation. Promoters displayed comparatively higher conservation of transcription factor motifs, whilst enhancers exhibited greater sequence diversity, broader genomic distributions and more variable motif repertoires. Comparative analysis revealed cis-regulatory divergence to be primarily temporal, with substantial chromatin remodelling and differential histone enrichment across development, while regulatory dynamics were highly conserved between forewing and hindwing tissues. Extending these experimentally characterised regulatory landscapes, a convolutional neural network was trained for sequence-based enhancer prediction, achieving test AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.909 and 0.913, respectively. Predictions across 34 Heliconiini assemblies displayed significant enrichment within independently characterised accessible chromatin and conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs), supporting their putative regulatory function. Overall, this study provides a large-scale characterisation of cis-regulatory dynamics and extends enhancer annotation across Heliconiini, providing a foundation for comparative investigations of regulatory conservation and diversification.

papers.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

papers.title: Crowdsourcing functional cell therapy binders from generative artificial intelligence.
papers.abstract: Over thirty years ago, structural biologists established the Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP) to rigorously assess methods for predicting protein structures from amino acid sequences. Participants submitted predictions before the corresponding experimental structures became publicly available (Moult et al, 1995). This framework established a common standard against which methodological advances could be measured. Its value became particularly evident at CASP14 in 2020, when AlphaFold2 produced predictions approaching experimental accuracy for many targets (Jumper et al, ; Pereira et al, 2021). CASP’s independent, prospective assessment enabled the community to recognize the scale of this advance by providing rapid, independent validation. The next generation of CASP-like open competitions is similarly poised to help discern the impact of emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods across several domains of biology, from genomics to protein design to therapeutic discovery. The implementation and results of one such effort, the Bits to Binders competition, are described in this issue of Molecular Systems Biology, where Kosonocky, Abel and colleagues evaluated 12,000 designed proteins as recognition domains for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells (Kosonocky et al, 2026). Generative AI is advancing protein binder design. Kosonocky, Abel and colleagues report on the Bits to Binders competition, which tested 12,000 designs in engineered T cells and identified promising candidates for future cell therapies. papers.title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA-Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Open-weight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.

papers.title: Integrative Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Explainable AI for Disease Mechanism and Biomarker Discovery in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Invasion is an early step in the metastatic spread of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet cells within a single tumour or cell line differ in their capacity to invade, and it is unclear which transcriptional features distinguish cells that invade from those that do not. We re-analysed the public single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset GSE329526, in which ClonMapper-barcoded MDA-MB-231 cells were separated in a transwell assay into invasive (five samples, 6,289 cells) and non-invasive (five samples, 5,983 cells) fractions and compared with the parental population (one sample, 3,022 cells). An initial cell-level analysis combined Wilcoxon differential expression, an XGBoost classifier with a random cell split, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Enrichr over-representation analysis. Because cells from the same sample are not independent, we then repeated the analysis at the sample level, using differential expression on sample means (five versus five), XGBoost with cross-validation that held out whole samples, a quality-control-metric baseline model, SHAP on held-out samples and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA). At the sample level, 6,651 of 11,727 tested genes differed between invasive and non-invasive samples (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05), including the ten top-ranked cell-level genes such as PHLDA2, ANTXR2, VIM and HMGA1 (FDR 0.0007 to 0.0022) and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulators TGFBR2, JAG1, SDCBP and WWTR1. With whole samples held out, XGBoost distinguished invasive from non-invasive cells with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92 (range across folds 0.89 to 0.95); removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes did not change performance (AUC 0.92), whereas a model using only four quality-control metrics reached 0.63, and every held-out invasive sample received a higher mean predicted probability of invasion (0.74 to 0.79) than every non-invasive sample (0.20 to 0.28). On held-out samples, SHAP ranked inflammatory and stress-response genes highest (CCL2, LGALS12, DUSP1, CXCL3, KYNU, CXCL2), and GSEA showed higher KRAS signalling (normalised enrichment score [NES] 2.30, FDR 0.001) and E2F targets (NES 1.62, FDR 0.038) and lower interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma responses (NES -1.97 and -1.65; FDR 0.001 and 0.019) in invasive samples. The ribosomal genes that dominated the original SHAP ranking were absent from the held-out ranking. Invasive MDA-MB-231 cells therefore carry a transcriptional state that is reproducible across independent transwell samples and involves EMT-related, inflammatory and proliferative programmes. Limitations include a single cell line, sequencing of the invasive and non-invasive populations in separate libraries and the absence of external validation; the candidate genes reported here are hypotheses that require confirmation in independent experiments and patient material.

papers.title: Building virtual cell dynamics that evolve with biological measurements
papers.abstract: Virtual cell models built from single-cell measurements need to predict how cells change over time, but new biological measurements often reveal dynamical relationships that existing models cannot express. Translating such measurements into dynamics therefore requires deciding what biological relation should be modeled, where it should enter the formulation and how its recovery should be validated. Here we present CellCompass, an agentic AI system that couples a scientific agent with an extensible dynamical engine for modeling state transitions and population change, along with fate and molecular readout. CellCompass reuses existing formulations when sufficient and designs, implements and refines new ones when experimental measurements introduce additional constraints. To assess this capability, we developed DynBench100, a benchmark of 100 simulated single-cell time-course scenarios with hidden dynamical ground truth. CellCompass achieved the highest aggregate performance among the tested general-purpose and biomedical agents across six dynamical tasks. Across four real single-cell studies, it retained an existing velocity-growth model to reconstruct context-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition and developed three new dynamical formulations for distinct experimental measurements. In drug-response data, incorporating metabolic RNA labeling reduced pulse-control identifiability error by 31.1%, revealing staged response programs and generating testable predictions for perturbing a candidate adaptive program. In hematopoietic lineage tracing, incorporating clonal barcodes improved clone-fate agreement by 54% over the strongest dynamical baseline, identifying early lineage priming among transcriptionally similar progenitors. Finally, in time-resolved CITE-seq data, CellCompass reduced future surface-protein distribution error by 13.2% for RNA-initialized trajectories, uncovering lineage-specific temporal offsets between transcriptional and protein programs. Together, CellCompass provides a framework in which virtual-cell dynamics can expand with the biological measurements used to constrain them.

papers.title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug--Target Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound--protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multi-level molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. \textcolor{black}{HierDTA represents each drug as an atom--motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase-domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis dataset across all metrics and attains the highest \(r_m^2\) of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7\% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components.} Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.

papers.title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
papers.abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

papers.title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
papers.abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
papers.abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficient transfer learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize antibacterial potency and minimize mammalian cytotoxicity without sequence leakage. Built upon ESM-2 (150M), our architecture incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into self-attention projections, fine-tuning approx 0.70% of model weights. To restore gradient interference originating from disparate membrane lysis mechanisms, we implement an adaptive multi-task loss guided by Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Evaluated across predefined QMAP benchmark splits enforcing a 60% maximal sequence identity threshold, our joint architecture remarkably outperforms conventional linear probes, tree-based regressors, and frozen foundational models. The framework achieves an E. coli potency rank correlation of {rho} = 0.6132 (r = 0.6816) and successfully elevates hemolytic toxicity correlation to {rho} = 0.5374 (r = 0.5541). To establish real world utility, we deploy the optimized joint network to screen a curated in silico library of 749 de-novo designed peptides, successfully isolating selective cationic-amphipathic candidates possessing Therapeutic Indices (TI = HC50/MIC) up to 144.03 while effectively deprioritizing broadly lytic motifs (TI < 2.0). These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation unlocks fine-grained bioactive structural semantics in foundational PLMs, providing an accurate, scalable framework for therapeutic peptide engineering.

papers.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
papers.abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

papers.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

papers.title: Probing Genomic Foundation Models with Splice-Variant Perturbations
papers.abstract: As benchmarks saturate, traditional validation methods fail to capture the probabilistic representations of genomic foundation models. This study probes self-supervised generalists (NTv3 650M, Evo2 40B, Genos 10B) alongside task-specific specialists (SpliceAI, AlphaGenome, Borzoi) using a mechanistically focused paradigm centered on expert-curated single-nucleotide substitutions within the splicing regions of the exon-rich OPA1 gene. Extending this analysis across the broader corpus of OPA1 mutations, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), and an independent 65-gene dataset of spliceogenic mutations demonstrates that foundation models not only match task-specific networks, but also generalize across mutation types. Training data scale, genetic diversity, and evolutionary context are key for capturing RNA splicing syntax, whereas sparse routing may constrain performance. Mechanistically, foundation models exhibit a compute asymmetry: Evo2 40B frontloads compute into massive parameter scale to resolve single-nucleotide variants within a narrow 425-bp context window, whereas the bidirectional NTv3 650M model and the Genos 10B mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture backload compute to inference, requiring spatial logit aggregation and vast context windows of up to 94 kb. Furthermore, accuracy may benefit from locus-specific thresholding rather than mutation-class calibration, exposing representation boundaries of the self-supervised models.

papers.title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
papers.abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altos-labs/scRM.

papers.title: Interactome-based deep learning and path-level decomposition reveal TGFβ-IFNα competition in MASH
papers.abstract: Dysregulated signaling drives Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH) through a complex crosstalk between pro- and anti-fibrotic cues. We previously observed potential competition between IFN-mediated JAK-STAT signaling and TGF{beta} in modulating MASH fibrosis, but the precise mechanism of that competition, and whether it can act directly on hepatocytes, is yet unknown. We used DT-LEMBAS, an interactome-based deep learning framework, training an ensemble of 50 models on drug-induced transcriptomics from primary human hepatocytes. The ensemble captured transcriptional changes induced by simulated receptor knockouts and aligned predicted profiles with known TGF{beta}- and IFN-induced phenotypes. Systematic simulations demonstrate their competitive modulation of MASH phenotype scores benchmarked against human cohorts. To extract mechanistic insights, we developed a gradient-based approach, where we computed the Jacobian of the used recurrent signaling network and applied chain rule decomposition to identify a four-node module of SMAD3, TP63, STAT2, and STAT3. Mechanistic hypotheses involving these canonical and non-canonical TF mediators were experimentally validated in primary hepatocyte spheroids. This work establishes a generalizable and scalable approach to decode large signaling neural networks into interpretable biological subnetworks.

papers.title: BLOOM: Biologically Informed Flow Matching for Transcriptomic Virtual Embryo Modeling
papers.abstract: Constructing a virtual embryo requires a generative representation of how heterogeneous cell populations change across developmental time. Here we introduce BLOOM, a biologically informed framework for conditional generation of developmental cell populations. BLOOM integrates temporal population context with developmental and regulatory priors through conditional flow matching to generate cell-expression distributions at queried stages in either temporal direction. Evaluation spans three mouse single-cell atlases covering prenatal development, visual-cortex maturation and multi-organ endothelial specialization. In comparisons with 22 time-series forecasting baselines, BLOOM ranks first for gene- and cell-expression correlations across all three datasets. Measured-stage evaluations support recovery of developmental expression patterns, population organization and marker-specific temporal relationships. Biological analyses connect these predictions to cell-state identities, gene programmes and regulatory associations. At unmeasured stages, interpolation and autoregressive history and future rollouts extend simulated expression dynamics between and beyond measured timepoints. Analyses of marker genes and temporal descriptors identify candidate differences in the timing of muscle-associated, neural and vascular-specialization programmes. Input-based gene perturbations further probe predicted responses of edited genes and associated molecular programmes across time. Together, BLOOM supports transcriptomic virtual embryo modeling by bridging temporal sampling gaps, exploring extended developmental trajectories and prioritizing gene-dependent hypotheses for experimental investigation.

papers.title: DNA language model GROVER learns sequence context in the human genome
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep-learning models that learn a sense of language on DNA have achieved a high level of performance on genome biological tasks. Genome sequences follow rules similar to natural language but are distinct in the absence of a concept of words. We established byte-pair encoding on the human genome and trained a foundation language model called GROVER (Genome Rules Obtained Via Extracted Representations) with the vocabulary selected via a custom task, next- k -mer prediction. The defined dictionary of tokens in the human genome carries best the information content for GROVER. Analysing learned representations, we observed that trained token embeddings primarily encode information related to frequency, sequence content and length. Some tokens are primarily localized in repeats, whereas the majority widely distribute over the genome. GROVER also learns context and lexical ambiguity. Average trained embeddings of genomic regions relate to functional genomics annotation and thus indicate learning of these structures purely from the contextual relationships of tokens. This highlights the extent of information content encoded by the sequence that can be grasped by GROVER. On fine-tuning tasks addressing genome biology with questions of genome element identification and protein–DNA binding, GROVER exceeds other models’ performance. GROVER learns sequence context, a sense for structure and language rules. Extracting this knowledge can be used to compose a grammar book for the code of life.

papers.title: Generative augmentation recovers prognostic disease signatures from underpowered transcriptomic datasets
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable gene-expression signatures from small transcriptomic datasets remains challenging. We present GeneLift, a framework that augments underpowered datasets using Gaussian mixture modelling in an analytically invertible latent space, retains genes reproducibly recovered across augmentations, and dates each against the literature using EvidenceClock, a Bayesian PubMed co-occurrence score, as antecedent, subsequent or unreported. Across 52 microarray and RNA-seq datasets spanning breast cancer, ovarian cancer, diabetes, sepsis and tuberculosis, GeneLift recovered candidate genes missed by standard differential expression analysis in all five diseases, including 326 in breast cancer and 976 in ovarian cancer. These candidates carried disease-specific literature support, including genes reported up to 18 years later such as the survival-associated ARL4D, and stratified overall survival in independent cohorts: TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC (log-rank P=6e-21 and 1e-42) and TCGA high-grade serous ovarian cancer (P=1e-37). In benchmarking, Gaussian mixture modelling outperformed more computationally intensive transformer-based generative adversarial networks. Together, GeneLift and EvidenceClock provide an efficient, reproducible framework for recovering prognostically informative signatures from underpowered transcriptomic studies.

papers.title: A universal deep-learning model for zinc finger design enables transcription factor reprogramming
papers.abstract: zinc finger (ZF) domains engineered to bind specific target sequences in the genome provide an effective strategy for programmable regulation of gene expression, with many potential therapeutic applications. However, the structurally intricate engagement of ZF domains with DNA has made their design challenging. Here we describe the screening of 49 billion protein-DNA interactions and the development of a deep-learning model, ZFDesign, that solves ZF design for any genomic target. ZFDesign is a modern machine learning method that models global and target-specific differences induced by a range of library environments and specifically takes into account compatibility of neighboring fingers using a novel hierarchical transformer architecture. We demonstrate the versatility of designed ZFs as nucleases as well as activators and repressors by seamless reprogramming of human transcription factors. These factors could be used to upregulate an allele of haploinsufficiency, downregulate a gain-of-function mutation or test the consequence of regulation of a single gene as opposed to the many genes that a transcription factor would normally influence.

papers.title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
papers.abstract: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

papers.title: Dali server: structural unification of protein families
papers.abstract: Protein structure is key to understanding biological function. Structure comparison deciphers deep phylogenies, providing insight into functional conservation and functional shifts during evolution. Until recently, structural coverage of the protein universe was limited by the cost and labour involved in experimental structure determination. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning revolutionized structural bioinformatics by providing accurate structural models of numerous protein families for which no structural information existed. The Dali server for 3D protein structure comparison is widely used by crystallographers to relate new structures to pre-existing ones. Here, we report two most recent upgrades to the web server: (i) the foldomes of key organisms in the AlphaFold Database (version 1) are searchable by Dali, (ii) structural alignments are annotated with protein families. Using these new features, we discovered a novel functionally diverse subgroup within the WRKY/GCM1 clan. This was accomplished by linking the structurally characterized SWI/SNF and NAM families as well as the structural models of the CG-1 family and uncharacterized proteins to the structure of Gti1/Pac2, a previously known member of the WRKY/GCM1 clan. The Dali server is available at http://ekhidna2.biocenter.helsinki.fi/dali. This website is free and open to all users and there is no login requirement.

papers.title: Accurate De Novo Prediction of Protein Contact Map by Ultra-Deep Learning Model
papers.abstract: Abstract Motivation Protein contacts contain key information for the understanding of protein structure and function and thus, contact prediction from sequence is an important problem. Recently exciting progress has been made on this problem, but the predicted contacts for proteins without many sequence homologs is still of low quality and not extremely useful for de novo structure prediction. Method This paper presents a new deep learning method that predicts contacts by integrating both evolutionary coupling (EC) and sequence conservation information through an ultra-deep neural network formed by two deep residual neural networks. The first residual network conducts a series of 1-dimensional convolutional transformation of sequential features; the second residual network conducts a series of 2-dimensional convolutional transformation of pairwise information including output of the first residual network, EC information and pairwise potential. By using very deep residual networks, we can model contact occurring patterns and very complex sequence-structure relationship and thus, obtain high-quality contact prediction regardless of how many sequence homologs are available for proteins in question. Results Our method greatly outperforms existing methods and leads to much more accurate contact-assisted folding. Tested on 105 CASP11 targets, 76 past CAMEO hard targets, and 398 membrane proteins, the average top L long-range prediction accuracy obtained our method, one representative EC method CCMpred and the CASP11 winner MetaPSICOV is 0.47, 0.21 and 0.30, respectively; the average top L/10 long-range accuracy of our method, CCMpred and MetaPSICOV is 0.77, 0.47 and 0.59, respectively. Ab initio folding using our predicted contacts as restraints but without any force fields can yield correct folds (i.e., TMscore>0.6) for 203 of the 579 test proteins, while that using MetaPSICOV- and CCMpred-predicted contacts can do so for only 79 and 62 of them, respectively. Our contact-assisted models also have much better quality than template-based models especially for membrane proteins. The 3D models built from our contact prediction have TMscore>0.5 for 208 of the 398 membrane proteins, while those from homology modeling have TMscore>0.5 for only 10 of them. Further, even if trained by only non-membrane proteins, our deep learning method works very well on membrane protein contact prediction. In the recent blind CAMEO benchmark, our fully-automated web server implementing this method successfully folded 5 targets with a new fold and only 0.3L-2.3L effective sequence homologs, including one β protein of 182 residues, one α+β protein of 125 residues, one α protein of 140 residues and one α protein of 217 residues and one α/β of 260 residues. Availability: http://raptorx.uchicago.edu/ContactMap/ Author Summary Protein contact prediction and contact-assisted folding has made good progress due to direct evolutionary coupling analysis (DCA). However, DCA is effectiv

papers.title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
papers.abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

papers.title: MAXWELL: Calibrating the probabilistic outputs of protein language models to the mutation-induced stability change landscape
papers.abstract: Designing mutations that enhance protein stability is a central goal in protein engineering. However, experimentally screening large numbers of candidate mutations is costly and time-consuming, creating a strong need for computational methods that can identify potentially stabilizing mutations. Among these approaches, protein language models are particularly promising because they learn context-dependent amino acid preferences from large-scale sequence and structure datasets. Nevertheless, most existing stability prediction methods use these models primarily as feature extractors and do not fully exploit the amino acid probability distributions they encode.
