Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO-GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO-GO forks. Sixteen life-sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-seq) and case-control genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence-dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC-Bench-public.

papers.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
papers.abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.

papers.title: Generative modeling of spatially resolved perturbation responses with CONCERT
papers.abstract: Spatial perturbation transcriptomics measures gene expression responses to genetic or chemical perturbations in intact tissue. Each response depends on the intrinsic state of a cell and on its niche, the neighboring cells through which perturbation effects propagate. Here we present CONCERT a niche-aware Gaussian process variational autoencoder that embeds each perturbation with the niche of the receiving cell and learns a spatial kernel for each perturbation, whose lengthscale sets how far the effect extends in tissue. We evaluate CONCERT in within-niche prediction, for held-out cells in the niche where a perturbation was measured, and in cross-slide prediction, for a slide from which the perturbation was withheld during training. On a SPAC-seq screen of hundreds of knockouts at single-cell resolution and on Perturb-map lung tumors at spot resolution, CONCERT predicts response magnitude and gene ranking more accurately than counterfactual models trained on dissociated cells, spatial perturbation models and spatial nearest neighbor aggregation. In dextran sodium sulfate colitis, where each mouse is sampled once, CONCERT reconstructs spatial gene expression at unmeasured time points, enabling longitudinal comparison that separates changes over time from differences between mice. The predictions recover the nonmonotonic course of injury, which peaks at day 9 and resolves by day 21. In ischemic stroke, CONCERT predicts responses to lesions of different sizes and locations, in single sections and across serial sections in three dimensions, and reproduces the expression patterns of the lesion core and perilesional tissue. Across lung tumor, colon and brain tissue, CONCERT predicts niche-aware counterfactual responses at locations where a perturbation was not measured and reconstructs missing spatial data.

papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

papers.title: Cross-modal transfer enables zero-shot prediction of drug responses across cell types
papers.abstract: Genetic perturbation responses capture the functional consequences of gene-level interventions, providing functional information for drug-response prediction beyond baseline gene expression. Within the same cellular context, genetic and chemical perturbations engage shared regulatory networks, providing a biological basis for transferring response information between perturbation modalities. Here we introduce GRAFT, a framework that combines genetic-to-chemical transfer with cross-context prediction to infer drug-induced transcriptional responses without drug measurements in the target context. Across benchmarked LINCS and external contexts, GRAFT improved response correlation, directional agreement and magnitude reconstruction over competing methods, particularly for drugs with context-dependent responses. GRAFT-Adapt further refines predictions of unmeasured responses using a small number of drug measurements from the target context. GRAFT-Atlas spans 13 cellular contexts and 7,856 drug catalog entries, comprising 102,128 predictions for drug-context combinations. The atlas captured recognizable pharmacological neighborhoods, shared functional programs, context-dependent transcriptional changes and structural-functional associations supported by molecular docking. Across ten iPSC lines from distinct donors, GRAFT identified candidate inter-donor differences, with functional support for selected candidates from measured genetic perturbation responses. Together, GRAFT enables perturbation-informed prediction and comparison of drug responses across cellular contexts.

papers.title: Interrogating contrastive learning embeddings for structure-based virtual screening: a case study on DrugCLIP
papers.abstract: Virtual screening has become central to early-stage drug discovery, and structure-based approaches have recently been reframed as a retrieval problem through contrastive learning methods such as DrugCLIP, which project protein pockets and ligands into a shared embedding space. However, what these abstract representations encode and how they relate to conventional notions of structural and chemical similarity remain unclear. Here we present a systematic dissection of DrugCLIP's latent space. We show that its pocket embeddings, despite not being explicitly trained for this task, achieve state-of-the-art performance in pocket similarity search while running over 10,000 times faster than existing structural descriptors. We further demonstrate that this embedding space is structurally coherent and robust to conformational variation. Ligand embeddings, by contrast, capture a pocket-aware notion of chemical similarity that extends beyond conventional fingerprint-based measures. Using a rigorous de-leakage benchmark, we show that DrugCLIP generalises beyond its fine-tuning set, retrieving the crystallographic ligand within the top 1% of a library of 48,999 compounds for 56.5% of 223 pockets with low protein sequence identity (SI [≤] 30%) and limited ligand chemical similarity (TS [≤] 0.7) to the fine-tuning set. Nevertheless, performance declines under increasingly realistic screening conditions, primarily due to differences in sidechain orientation across apo, holo and AlphaFold-predicted structures, and mismatches in pocket residue composition when using predicted pockets. These findings delineate the practical limits of DrugCLIP's applicability, highlight accurate pocket identification and representation as key factors for improving performance, and provide a transferable framework for interpreting the latent spaces of related contrastive pocket-ligand models. Together, these results offer insight to guide the refinement of existing methods and the development of future contrastive screening approaches.

papers.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.
